lines.text: גבל 175 גבע
southwards to Petra, and still called by
the Arabs جبال Jebâl. In Judith 3, 1
Lat. Vers. and also in the writings of the
Crusaders, it is called Syria Sobal; by
Josephus, Euseb. and Steph. Byz. Γοβο-
λῖτις, Γεβαληνή, Γάβαλα. See Bibl. Res.
n Palest. II. p. 552.
גְּבֻל see גְּבוּל.
גַּבְלֹת f. (r. גָּבַל) wreathen work, twist-
ed like cords, see the root Kal no. 1. Ex.
28, 22 and thou shalt make upon the
breast-plate שַׁרְשׁוֹת גַּבְלֻת מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבֹת זָהָב
טָהוֹר wreathed chains (i. e. like cords),
braided or laced work of pure gold;
Sept. well κροσσοὺς συμπεπλεγμένους.
Ex. 39, 15. The same thing is expressed
in Ex. 28, 14, and two chains of pure gold,
מִגְבָּלוֹת תַּעֲשֶׂה אֹתָם מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבֹת wreathed
(like cords) shalt thou make them, braid-
ed work; Sept. καταμεμιγμένα (ἐν ἄν-
θεσι). Most prob. we are to understand
small chains made of gold threads or
wire twisted or braided together like
cords; and then מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבֹת is added by
way of epexegesis.
* גָּבַן not used in Heb. 1. to be gib-
bous, curved, see under גָּבַב no. 1; so of
the body, see גִּבֵּן; of a mountain, see
גַּבְנֻנִּים; of the eye-brow, arch of the eye,
see Syr. and Chald. גְּבִינָא.
2. Trop. of the body, to shrink together
from fear, terror, Arab. جَبَنَ and جَبُنَ
to be timid, fearful; Act. to terrify.
3. Of milk, to curdle, to coagulate;
comp. Germ. die Milch erschrickt, i. e.
curdles. Hence גְּבִינָה curdled milk,
cheese.
גִּבֵּן m. adj. gibbous, hunch-backed,
גַּבְנֻנִּים m. plur. (r. גָּבַן no. 1) heights,
summits, q. d. humps, hummocks of a
mountain. Ps. 68, 16 הַר־גַּבְנֻנִּים הַר־בָּשָׁן O
mount of summits, mount of Bashan;
and v. 17 הָרִים גַּבְנֻנִּים by apposit. ye
mountains, summits, i. e. abounding
in summits. — Comp. Talm. גַּבְנוּנִית
crown of the head, summit; Syr. ܓܒܺܝܢܳܐ
summit of a mountain, arch of the eye-
brow; Arab. جَبَّانَة rough uneven coun-
try; also a cemetery, so called from the
sepulchral mounds, tumuli.
* גָּבַע not found in the verb, kindr.
with the roots גָּבַב q. v. גָּבַהּ, גָּבַח, etc.
and signifying to be high, like a moun-
tain, hill; and spec. to be arched, con-
vex, round, like a cup, the top of the
head, etc. see גָּבִיעַ, גִּבְעֹל, מִגְבָּעָה. Comp.
Arab. قَبٌّ head, chief, Gr. κεφαλή, Lat.
caput, capo, all which flow from the same
primary source.
Deriv. גָּבִיעַ, מִגְבָּעָה, and the six here
following.
גֶּבַע (hill) Geba, Gaba, pr. n. of a
Levitical city in Benjamin, Josh. 18, 24.
21, 17; situated on the northern border
of the kingdom of Judah, 2 K. 23, 8. Zech.
14, 10. More fully גֶּבַע בִּנְיָמִין 1 Sam.
13, 16. 1 K. 15, 22. It was near to
Gibeah (גִּבְעָה no. 2. a), towards the
northeast, Is. 10, 29. Josh. 18, 24. 28.
From these passages too it is evident
that Geba and Gibeah could not have
been the same place; although in Judg.
20, 10. 33, גֶּבַע is inaccurately put for
גִּבְעָה; comp. the context. [Now جبع
Jeb'a; see Bibl. Res. in Palest. II. p.
113, 114. Biblioth. Sac. 1844, p. 598 sq.
גִּבְעָא (hill) Gibea, pr. n. m. 1 Chr.
גִּבְעָה f. (r. גָּבַע) plur. גְּבָעוֹת 1. a hill,
גִּבְעֹת עוֹלָם everlasting hills, i. e. ever the
same from the creation until now, Gen.
49, 26. Job 15, 7 לִפְנֵי גְבָעוֹת חוֹלָלְתָּ wast
thou brought forth before the hills? Prov.
8, 25. גִּבְעַת יְהוָֹה the hill of Jehovah, i. e.
Zion, Ez. 34, 26, comp. Is. 31, 4. Many
of the hills in Palestine were distinguish-
ed by pr. names; as אַמָּה, גָּרֵב, חֲכִילָה.
2. Meton. a city on a hill; comp. the
termination dunum in the early names of
cities in Germany, France, and Britain,
which in Celtic signifies a hill, as Au-
gustodunum, Cæsarodunum, Lugdunum,
etc. Hence as pr. n. Gibeah:
a) גִּבְעַת בִּנְיָמִין 1 Sam. 13, 2. 15, ג׳ בְּנֵי
בִּנְיָמִין 2 Sam. 23, 29, Gibeah of Benja-
min; likewise called גִּבְעַת שָׁאוּל Gibeah
of Saul 1 Sam. 11, 4; גִּבְעַת הָאֱלֹהִים
1 Sam. 10, 5, comp. 10; also κατ᾿ ἐξοχήν
הַגִּבְעָה Gibeah, Hos. 5, 8. 9, 9. 10, 9;

line_status.note: The sixth letter is an 'h' whose ascender failed to ink, so it looks like 'n' in the scan; the word is southwards, so Reading A is correct and B copies the print defect.

The line begins with a bare "n" — no "i" is printed before it. The left margin is fully within the crop (the "C" of "Crusaders" above starts further left), and the space where the "i" of "in" should be is blank, so the type either dropped out or failed to ink. Reading A supplies the intended "in" but not what is printed; Reading B records the page as it stands.

Under the bet of the headword the print shows three diagonal dots (qibbuts, גְּבֻל), not a qamets as in Reading A; this is the defective spelling cross-referenced to plene גְּבוּל. The final period is set off by a visible space, as in Reading B.

The lamed of the headword carries a single dot printed above/left of its upright (holem), with no three-dot qibbuts beneath it; the print reads גַּבְלֹת, not גַּבְלֻת. Everything else in both readings matches the print.

In the first word a narrow vertical stroke (vav) is printed between lamed and tav, with the holem dot sitting over it rather than over the lamed: plene מִגְבָּלוֹת, not defective מִגְבָּלֹת. All other points agree in both readings and match the print.

The printed word is גְּבִינָא (gimel with dagesh, bet, yod, nun with qamets, aleph) — "cheese", fitting the root גָּבַן. Reading B's גַּבְרִיָא inserts a resh that is not printed and misplaces the yod/nun; the crop clearly shows the yod-nun-aleph ending.

Decisive difference is the vowel on the bāʾ of each Arabic form: the first word (left of "and") shows a fatḥa stroke over ب (جَبَنَ), while the second word (right of "and") shows the small comma-shaped ḍamma over ب (جَبُنَ). Reading A reverses the two.
Under the first gimel of גביע the print shows a qamets (T-shaped mark with a stem), not a shewa; Reading B's גְּבִיעַ is wrong. All other points and the item order agree in both readings.

The mark stacked above the final ب is a shadda with a dammatan (tanwīn) on top, not a bare shadda — the tall two-tier glyph with the curled upper element is the shadda+dammatan combination, so Reading B's قَبٌّ is what is printed.
